builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
summary: The benchmark and its skills replace ad-hoc prompting of coding agents for clinical variable derivation with versioned, clinician-reviewable operational specifications covering item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output grain. Cost is the clinician effort to author and maintain these specifications plus per-task agent runs in a Docker-isolated environment; the open-source benchmark itself runs on a single machine with third-party APIs. Failure modes include agents producing partially correct outputs that pass few strict checks, unchanged row selection (key F1 +0.003), and residual risk that gains partly reflect schema memorization rather than specification use.
rationale: The evidence shows the practical lever for constrained teams is writing complete operational specifications for derivation tasks, which is cheap to adopt, but the benchmark is clinically specific and strict success rates are low, so it warrants workload-specific validation rather than direct adoption.
technique: Clinician-reviewed specification skills for EHR coding agents

claims.statement: The benchmark and its skills replace ad-hoc prompting of coding agents for clinical variable derivation with versioned, clinician-reviewable operational specifications covering item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output grain. Cost is the clinician effort to author and maintain these specifications plus per-task agent runs in a Docker-isolated environment; the open-source benchmark itself runs on a single machine with third-party APIs. Failure modes include agents producing partially correct outputs that pass few strict checks, unchanged row selection (key F1 +0.003), and residual risk that gains partly reflect schema memorization rather than specification use.

Skills raise task reward by 0.136 over baseline (26/28 tasks improving); specification completeness alone accounts for +0.162 on a control subset, with skill format adding only +0.024 (indistinguishable from zero); strict full-pass rates remain low (25/280 with skills).
